vignette:
He is 25 now, a quiet North American man who works as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel, moving through other people's spaces with a practiced care that makes him nearly invisible. When he begins talking about his childhood, he does it in fragments at first, as if each piece has to be tested before it can be set down. He grows up with a caregiver whose moods rule the house. As a boy, he learns to listen for the smallest signs: the weight of footsteps in the hallway, the sharp closing of a cabinet, the scrape of a chair pushed back too quickly. Violence often arrives before words do. He is grabbed by the arm hard enough to leave finger-shaped bruises, slapped for being "disrespectful," shoved into walls for small mistakes that other children would barely notice. He remembers trying to keep the house perfect, believing that if he stayed quiet enough, useful enough, he might stay safe.

Even then, his body never really believes in safety. At school, he startles when teachers raise their voices, even if they are speaking to someone else. He has trouble concentrating because part of him is always listening for danger. He avoids bringing friends home, embarrassed by the tension in the house and terrified that they will either witness the abuse or somehow make it worse. At night, he lies awake rehearsing the next day, thinking about what to say, what not to say, how to move through each room without attracting attention. When he does fall asleep, he wakes quickly, heart pounding, unsure for a moment whether he is still a child in that house.

As he gets older, he spends more time away whenever he can. He stays late at school, wanders stores, volunteers to help teachers clean up after class. There is relief in chores. Wiping a desk, lining up supplies, taking out trash-these are small tasks with clear endings, unlike the chaos at home. By his mid-teens, he has become exceptionally good at reading other people's moods. Adults describe him as mature, polite, "no trouble at all." He hears this as both compliment and warning. Being easy to manage has always been his strategy for survival.

He leaves home as soon as he can. From the outside, adulthood looks like freedom, but his body carries the old rules with it. In shared apartments and temporary jobs, he is the one who apologizes too quickly, who freezes when someone sounds irritated, who replays ordinary interactions for hours afterward, searching for signs that he has done something wrong. He tells himself the past is over, yet sudden movements still make him flinch. A slammed door can erase the present in an instant. The heat rises in his chest, his muscles tense, and for a few seconds he is no longer a grown man in a hallway or break room; he is back in that house, bracing.

Housekeeping suits him in ways he understands and ways he does not mention right away. He likes the structure: cart stocked, beds stripped, towels folded, surfaces restored. There is comfort in making disorder look untouched. He can enter a room, notice every detail, and leave no sign of himself behind. Coworkers appreciate that he is dependable and rarely complains. What they do not always see is how exhausting the work can be when guests are still inside the room, when a man speaks sharply from across the bed, or when he hears raised voices through a door. He smiles, says "No problem," and keeps moving, but afterward his hands shake while he refolds linens in the service hallway. If a guest leaves a mess that feels aggressive-broken items, liquor bottles scattered, furniture overturned-he becomes flooded with a familiar dread that he cannot easily explain.

He is single, though not because he does not want closeness. He wants it badly and distrusts it at the same time. When someone shows interest in him, he becomes watchful. A delayed text can ruin an entire evening; a joking insult can land like a threat. He often pulls away before the other person has the chance to. He tells himself he is independent, but there are nights in his apartment when the silence feels thin and exposed. He checks the lock more than once. He keeps the television on to fill the room with sound. Sleep comes late. Some nights he wakes sweating from dreams in which he is small again, trapped in the old house, trying to predict an explosion that never fully arrives but never stops threatening to.

In conversation, he minimizes what happened to him, then catches himself. He says other people had it worse. He says his caregiver "just had a temper." But when he describes being cornered in the kitchen as a child, or the humiliation of trying not to cry while being hit, the cost of that temper becomes visible. He lives in a constant negotiation between wanting to forget and being unable to. Crowded places make him scan exits. Criticism, even mild and deserved, can leave him nauseated and ashamed for hours. He is often tired, though he rarely rests. Cleaning his own apartment can become compulsive when he is overwhelmed, as if order might do what safety never did.

What stands out most is how much of his life is organized around preventing something that is no longer happening. He moves carefully, listens closely, keeps himself useful, and braces for harm even in ordinary moments. Part of him knows he is 25, employed, living on his own, answerable to no caregiver now. Another part still waits for footsteps outside the door.
